Row.Text: Toyotomi Hideyoshi, one of the three great rulers of the fractured Sengoku era of Japan, is a figure defined by ambition and cunning, loyalty and audacity. Rising from obscurity, Toyotomi became kanpaku (regent, often de facto ruler) of Japan and harbored dreams of taking down the world’s mightiest empire, Ming China.

Hideyoshi was not born Toyotomi – he was Hiyoshimaru, the son of an ashigaru (foot soldier), and his early life as a commoner is not recorded. Over time, he rose from a wandering adventurer to a servant for a minor lord. In the chaos of the late 16th century, during the endless wars of the Sengoku period, he entered the orbit of daimyo Oda Nobunaga as a sandal-bearer. Toyotomi’s great feat, though, was a daring raid on Inabayama Castle, the decisive battle that would solidify the Oda clan’s victory over their rivals. Oda Nobunaga, in his typical aggressive style, had prepared an all-out assault, but Toyotomi (then going by the name of Kinoshita Tokichiro) and a crew of around ten men scaled the mountain behind the castle by moonlight. When Oda’s assault came at dawn, Toyotomi’s team was already inside, and they opened the gates. The assault – and a subsequent record of victories for Oda – earned him a general’s position.

Oda was assassinated in 1582 when a vassal betrayed him. Toyotomi hunted down and killed the rebel and claimed Oda’s mantle. The next years were ones of conquest and consolidation, and Toyotomi faced off against the peasant armies of the Ikko-Ikki, groups of warrior monks, and would-be rulers. In 1585, Toyotomi finally claimed the highest title available to him – kanpaku (regent) – and was given the clan name Toyotomi.

In 1591, the conquest of Japan was complete, and Toyotomi set his sights abroad, seeing Ming China as a target for further expansion – as well as, allegedly, India and Southeast Asia. Conquering Ming, though, meant landing troops, and Toyotomi saw Joseon as the likely beachhead for a larger force. As famed as he was in persuasion, Toyotomi could not sway the Korean ambassadors to betray their overlords in Ming, so Toyotomi turned toward more aggressive means. He launched two invasions – what are known as the Imjin Wars – as an attempt to secure the peninsula. Although Toyotomi’s forces occupied much of Korea, in the end each attempt was defeated, as the Korean navy under Admiral Yi Sun-sin outflanked and outwitted the Japanese fleets, unfamiliar as they were with the Korean coast, and cut off Japanese supply lines.

Toyotomi died at the age of 61, expressing regret over his ambition and cautioning his successors to check the rising influence and power of yet another ambitious warlord – Tokugawa Ieyasu. In this, they were unsuccessful. Tokugawa would prove to be the final, and ultimate, bringer of peace to war-torn Japan, and the subsequent Edo period would be marked by the Tokugawa clan.

Toyotomi is a complicated figure. Rising from obscurity and without a lineage or clan to support his ambitions required a careful attention to what made power attractive. For Toyotomi, it was not only effectiveness in strategy, but also a cultivation of the arts. He became a patron of tea ceremony and especially of Noh theater – a refined and exclusive form of highly stylized performance. In this way, he not only embodied the skill of a warrior-lord, but also the refinement of a lord of culture. He involved himself deeply in administration as well and, as kanpaku, spoke with the authority of the emperor. Though he could never be emperor himself, he arranged where imperial power went and what it did.

Personally, despite the attention toward a cultivated appearance and his careful skill in strategy, Toyotomi was capable of fits of rage. His disrespect toward the Korean ambassadors may have sabotaged his Ming conquest plans, and once, famously, he furiously demanded that a subordinate, the tea master Sen No Rikyu, commit suicide. His impulsiveness could be a boon, too – extending as it did to improvisation in his otherwise carefully-staged Noh performances. Historians and contemporary observers alike both note that the physically active and emotionally expressive Toyotomi cut a sharp contrast with the formal, still character of previous (and subsequent) Japanese monarchs. Divisive as he was, Toyotomi was vibrantly present.

Toyotomi Hideyoshi, born from nothing and arising with dreams of world conquest, is remembered for his ambition. But his legacy lives on in the pageantry of Japanese high culture, and he helped set the stage not only for the administration of the coming Edo era, but also its arts.
